payload.rationale: Historically, measles was declared eliminated in the US in 2000. The highest number of annual cases since then was 1,282 in 2019. Reaching over 6,000 cases in a single year would require a nearly five-fold increase over the worst recent outbreak, which would necessitate a catastrophic breakdown in herd immunity and public health response across multiple large population centers. While vaccine hesitancy has increased in some areas, school mandates and rapid public health responses to outbreaks generally keep case counts in the dozens or hundreds. Strongest reason my estimate could be too high: Public health infrastructure and existing high baseline MMR vaccination rates make an outbreak of this scale virtually impossible without a fundamental change in the virus or society. Strongest reason it could be too low: A coordinated, nationwide drop in vaccination rates combined with delayed public health responses could theoretically allow a highly contagious virus like measles to spread rapidly through susceptible clusters, leading to unprecedented post-elimination numbers.
limitations: No current research or case count data supplied for 2026.
Relies on historical baseline data prior to the forecast cutoff.
